summary: A proposal to extend the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol so that one user program could tell file servers at two other sites to cooperate, passing files between them directly. The authors motivated it with programs that extend a user's commands across several hosts. It builds on RFC 354 and its updates.

eli5.summary: Instead of carrying a package from one house to another yourself, you phone both houses and let them hand it to each other.

questions: what is the ftp lstn command
how can two ftp servers transfer a file directly
subtitle: A 1973 proposal to let two FTP servers exchange a file directly, steered by a third program.

tldr.problem: ARPANET FTP allows a third host to take part but gives no way for the process at that third site to be the FTP server there, so a program cannot make two servers pass a file directly.
tldr.mechanism: Add one new command, LSTN, and tweak SOCK, APPE, RETR and STOR, so a server can be told to listen for a data connection as if it were a user.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a suggestion for an extension. It reports a related experimental RSEXEC program running on TENEXs for about 8 months using a private protocol.

today: RFC 438 is a 1973 proposal and its status is listed as Unknown. Nothing in its text says whether the extension was adopted.

sections.title: Why Servers Need to Talk
sections.content:
FTP, as specified by RFC 354 and updated by RFC 385, RFC 414 and RFC 418, lets a third host take part but not its FTP server. The authors point to a Resource Sharing Executive (RSEXEC), a command interpreter that extends a user's commands across sites.

If a user asks it to append a file at SITE1 to a file at SITE2, the natural way is to open FTP control connections to both servers and have them share one data connection. FTP cannot do that today, mainly because it treats the two ends of a data connection asymmetrically, one as server and one as user.
sections.eli5: A helper program wants two faraway computers to swap a file with each other. The old rules only let one of them act as the host, so they could not.

sections.title: The LSTN Extension
sections.content:
Two fixes are possible: make data connection setup symmetric, or let a server set up its end as if it were a user. The RFC picks the second because it needs fewer changes.

The new LSTN (Listen) command, written LSTN <direction> CRLF with S for send or R for receive, asks the server to allocate a data socket. The server either refuses or returns the socket number, for which the 255 data socket reply could be used. A following STOR, RETR or APPE makes the server listen for an RFC on that socket and answer with a matching one. The connection then lasts as long as an ordinary one.
sections.eli5: One server is told, "wait by this door." The other is told which door to knock on. When they meet, the file passes between them.

sections.title: SOCK Changes and the Example
sections.content:
SOCK changes in two ways. On success its reply must be the 255 reply right away, so the user can pass the server's socket to the other site. After an LSTN, SOCK also names the only host and socket from which the server will accept a connection, which protects the transfer.

In the RFC's example, the RSEXEC sends LSTN R to SITE2 and gets socket X. It tells SITE1 SOCK SITE2,X and receives socket Y. It then tells SITE2 SOCK SITE1,Y, and finally sends RETR PROG1.PL1 to SITE1 and APPE PROG2.PL1 to SITE2.
sections.eli5: The helper tells each server the other's address, then says "send" to one and "receive" to the other.

messages.label: SOCK SITE2,X
messages.note: SITE1 replies with socket Y in its 255 reply.
